lessons.title: Getting ready to harvest
lessons.html:
Harvesting by hand

Many crops in South Africa are still picked by hand: apples, pears, citrus, table grapes, tomatoes, green beans, cabbages, butternut, sweet potatoes and many more. Hand harvesting is careful work. A bruised or dirty fruit loses value, and the farmer loses money.

Is the crop ready?

Your supervisor will tell you which block to pick and what the crop must look like. Crops are picked when they are ripe enough for their market. Signs can be:

  • Colour: for example, the background colour of an apple, or orange colour on citrus.
  • Size: some crops are only picked when they pass a size ring or gauge.
  • Firmness and feel: a cabbage head must be firm.
  • Easy release: a ripe pear or apple often comes off easily when lifted and twisted.

Only pick what you are told to pick. Leave the rest for the next round.

Equipment

  • Picking bags or buckets that are clean and not damaged.
  • Clippers or knives for crops that are cut, such as grapes, citrus and cabbage.
  • Ladders for tall trees.
  • Clean bins or crates.
  • Size gauges or colour charts if needed.

Check your equipment before you start. Sharp clippers make clean cuts. Blunt clippers tear stems.

Hygiene before picking

Food that is eaten raw must be kept clean. Wash your hands with soap after using the toilet and before you start picking. Do not pick if you are sick with diarrhoea or vomiting; tell your supervisor. Cover cuts on your hands. Do not eat, smoke or spit in the rows.

lessons.title: Picking, handling and safety
lessons.html:
Picking the right way

  1. Hold the fruit in your whole hand, not with your fingertips, so you do not leave finger bruises.
  2. Lift and twist, or cut the stem as you were shown. Do not pull fruit off, because it can tear the skin or break the branch.
  3. For cut crops, cut the stem short and clean so it does not poke holes in other fruit.
  4. Place the fruit gently in the bag. Do not throw or drop it.
  5. Empty the bag gently into the bin, close to the bottom. Do not tip it from high up.
  6. Do not overfill bins or crates. Fruit pressed under a lid is damaged.

Sorting in the field

Leave out fruit that is rotten, badly damaged, or has fallen on the ground, unless your supervisor says otherwise. Fallen fruit can carry soil and germs.

Keeping the crop cool

Once picked, crops start to lose quality. Put full bins in the shade and get them to the packhouse or cold room as quickly as possible. Never leave bins standing in the sun.

Ladder safety

  • Check the ladder for broken steps or legs before you use it.
  • Stand it on firm, flat ground and lean it into the tree properly.
  • Do not stand on the top step.
  • Do not reach too far to the side. Climb down and move the ladder.
  • Keep three points of contact: two feet and one hand, or two hands and one foot.

Look after yourself

Drink water often on hot days and wear a hat. Lift full crates by bending your knees, keeping your back straight and the load close to your body. Watch out for snakes and bees in the trees. Report any injury straight away.

Recording

Many farms count bins or crates per picker with a card or scanner. Make sure your count is recorded correctly at the end of each row or bin.

Key points

  • Pick only what is ripe and what you were told to pick.
  • Handle the crop gently: no dropping, throwing or overfilling.
  • Wash your hands and keep the crop clean.
  • Keep picked crops in the shade and move them quickly.
  • Use ladders safely and lift with your legs.
